Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Question: Thanks for making time, Jordan. I've looked through your portfolio and I'd love to just have a conversation about how you actually work. Less about polished case studies, more about the messy reality. Sound good?
Answer: Yeah, absolutely. I appreciate that, honestly. I've only been doing this professionally for about ten months, so my process is still... evolving, I guess. But I'm happy to be real about it.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: design_handoff, design_metrics, prototyping, stakeholder_management, user_research
Question: That's exactly what I want to hear. So let's start big picture. Walk me through a project from the initial brief to the final handoff. Where did your process change or break down?
Answer: Sure. So the biggest end-to-end project I've owned was redesigning the onboarding flow for a fintech app I worked on during my contract role. The brief came from the product manager, and it was pretty loose: "new users are dropping off during signup, fix it." That was basically it. I started by looking at the analytics we had, which was just Mixpanel funnel data. I could see where people were leaving, but not really why. I wanted to do user interviews, but the timeline was three weeks and my manager kind of said, "We don't really have time for that, just use what we have." So I pulled some session recordings from Hotjar instead, which gave me something to work with. From there I sketched out a few flow variations on paper, brought them to the PM, and we narrowed it down. I moved into Figma, built out the screens, did a couple of informal feedback rounds with two other designers on the team, and then handed it off to engineering. Where it broke down... honestly, the handoff was rough. I built the designs in Figma but I didn't spec out edge cases well enough. Like, what happens if someone enters an invalid routing number? What does the error state look like? I had the happy path nailed but the engineers kept coming back to me with questions I should have anticipated. So the "handoff" ended up being this two-week back-and-forth that wasn't really planned for. I've gotten a lot better about building out error states and edge cases since then, but that project taught me the hard way.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Question: That's a really common thing, even for experienced designers. The edge case problem never fully goes away. Okay, so question one: how do you decide when a design is "done enough" to ship?
Answer: This is something I genuinely struggle with. My instinct is to keep iterating because I can always see things I'd tweak. But what I've learned, mostly from my PM pushing back, is that "done enough" usually means: does it solve the core problem we identified, is it usable for the majority case, and can engineering actually build it in the time we have? I try to ask myself, "If we ship this tomorrow, will users be confused or blocked?" If the answer is no, it's probably good enough. The visual polish, the micro-interactions, the perfect spacing, those matter, but they're not worth holding up a release if the underlying experience is solid. That said, I've definitely shipped things too early before. There was a settings page I designed where I knew the information architecture was off, but I let myself get talked into shipping it because "we can iterate later." And then we never went back to it. So now I push harder on structural issues even if I'm more flexible on surface-level stuff.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: design_metrics, prototyping, user_research
Question: That's a good distinction, structure versus surface. Okay, what does your research phase typically look like, and when have you skipped it? What happened?
Answer: Honestly? My research phase is usually lighter than I want it to be. In a perfect world, I'd do user interviews, competitive analysis, maybe a survey. In reality, what I usually end up doing is pulling analytics data, looking at session recordings, reading through support tickets, and doing a quick competitive scan of three or four similar products. I've skipped research almost entirely once, and it was bad. It was a feature for bulk-uploading contacts. The PM had a really specific vision and was confident about what users wanted, so I just jumped straight into wireframes based on his spec. Turns out the mental model he had, dragging and dropping a CSV file, didn't match how most of our users actually thought about it. They wanted to copy and paste from a spreadsheet directly into the app. We found that out after launch when support tickets spiked. We had to redesign it two months later, and the second time I actually talked to five users before starting. Took two extra days upfront but saved us weeks. So now even when I'm pressured to skip research, I try to do at least some lightweight version. Even five 15-minute calls can change your direction completely.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Question: The copy-paste versus CSV thing is such a classic example. People's mental models are never what you assume. Alright, tell me about a design decision you made that the team pushed back on. How did you handle it?
Answer: Yeah, so on that same onboarding project, I wanted to break the signup flow into multiple steps, one thing per screen. Name, then email, then password, then phone number. I felt strongly about it because all the UX research I'd read said progressive disclosure reduces cognitive load and improves completion rates. But the engineering lead pushed back hard. He said it would mean more API calls, more state management, more things to break. The PM was also hesitant because it meant more screens to maintain. They both wanted a single-page form. At first I was kind of defensive about it, I'll be honest. I felt like I was "right" from a UX perspective and they were just thinking about engineering convenience. But then I stepped back and realized I was treating it as a debate to win instead of a problem to solve together. What I ended up doing was proposing a middle ground: a single page, but visually chunked into sections with clear labels, and we'd auto-scroll to the next section as they completed each one. It wasn't my ideal solution, but it addressed the cognitive load issue without creating the engineering complexity. And when we shipped it, the completion rate actually went up 12%, so it worked well enough. The lesson I took from that was to lead with the problem, not the solution. Instead of saying "we need to split this into five screens," I should have said "users are overwhelmed by the form, how might we reduce that feeling?" and then let the team arrive at a solution together.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: stakeholder_management
Question: That's mature for someone ten months in. Okay, describe a time you had to design for constraints you disagreed with, whether technical, business, or timeline. What tradeoffs did you make?
Answer: The biggest one was a timeline constraint. We had a client dashboard that needed a reporting feature, and the stakeholder wanted it done in a week and a half. That's design and engineering combined. I knew a proper reporting tool needed filtering, date range pickers, exportable data, and probably some data visualization. There was no way to do all of that well in a week and a half. I disagreed with the timeline, and I said so, but the business commitment had already been made to the client. So it was happening regardless. What I did was triage pretty aggressively. I made a list of everything the feature could include and then ranked it by what would make the feature useful at a minimum-viable level versus what would make it delightful. We shipped with a simple table view with date filtering and CSV export. No charts, no saved filters, no customizable columns. It was bare-bones but functional. The tradeoff was that I knew users would find it underwhelming compared to competitors. And they did. We got feedback about wanting charts and more flexibility. But we also got feedback that the data itself was valuable and the export feature was used daily. So the core decision to prioritize data access over data presentation turned out to be the right call for V1. I think the tradeoff I'm least comfortable with was cutting the empty states. When there was no data for a date range, it just showed a blank table. No message, no illustration, nothing. That's a small thing but it makes the product feel unfinished, and we still haven't gone back to fix it.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: user_research
Question: Empty states are the thing everyone cuts and no one goes back to. I feel that. How do you measure whether a design worked?
Answer: I'll be honest, this is an area I'm still developing. The quantitative side I'm okay with: I look at the metrics we defined at the start of the project. Completion rates, drop-off points, time on task, support ticket volume for that feature. For the onboarding redesign, we tracked signup completion rate and it improved by about 18%, so that felt like a clear win. But the qualitative side is harder for me. I haven't been great about setting up post-launch user interviews to understand the "why" behind the numbers. Like, our numbers went up, but I don't fully know which specific changes drove that. Was it the simplified form? The new copy? The progress indicator? I can hypothesize based on the A/B test data, but we didn't instrument it granularly enough to isolate individual changes. Going forward, something I want to get better at is defining success criteria at the start of a project, not just "improve the metric," but "we believe [this specific change] will [cause this specific behavior] because [this reason]." That way I can actually validate my design rationale, not just the outcome.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: design_handoff, design_systems, prototyping, responsive_design
Question: That hypothesis-driven framing is exactly right. It's something a lot of people never get to, so the fact that you're thinking about it now is great. Okay, how do you hand off designs to developers? What's gone wrong?
Answer: Right now my handoff process is Figma-based. I try to set up a dedicated handoff page in the file with the final screens, annotated with notes for anything that isn't obvious. I use auto-layout and components so the dev inspect panel actually gives useful spacing and sizing info. And then I do a synchronous walkthrough with the engineering team, usually 30 minutes, where I go screen by screen. What's gone wrong... a lot, honestly. The thing I mentioned earlier about missing edge cases is the biggest one. But there have been other issues too. One time, I was using a component from our design system in Figma that had been updated in code but not in the Figma library. So what I was designing with visually didn't match what the engineers were building with. The button padding was different, the font weight was slightly off. It shipped looking subtly wrong and we didn't catch it until QA. Another thing that's tripped me up is responsive behavior. I'll design for desktop and maybe one mobile breakpoint, but I won't spec out what happens at tablet widths or weird in-between sizes. The engineers then have to make judgment calls, and sometimes their judgment is different from mine. Not wrong, just different. So now I try to at least annotate the rules: "this sidebar collapses at 768px," "these cards go from three columns to two at 1024px," that kind of thing. I'm also learning that the walkthrough meeting matters more than the Figma annotations. Engineers ask questions I'd never think to annotate. "What happens if this text is 200 characters long?" "What if the user has no profile photo?" Having that conversation live catches so much.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: design_systems, prototyping, stakeholder_management
Question: Design system drift between Figma and code is one of those problems that haunts every team. Good that you're aware of it. Okay, tell me about a time a stakeholder wanted something you thought was a bad user experience. What did you do?
Answer: The clearest example was when our CEO wanted to add a promotional banner to the top of the dashboard. Like a full-width, bright-colored banner advertising a new feature, and he wanted it to be non-dismissible. He wanted it to stay there until the user clicked through to the feature page. I thought it was a terrible idea. The dashboard is where users go to do their core work, and a permanent banner that you can't close is basically a punishment for not being interested in a feature. It felt like the kind of thing that would annoy power users, who are our most valuable segment. But I also recognized that I was a ten-month-in junior designer and he was the CEO, and maybe he had context I didn't about the business need to drive adoption of this feature. So instead of saying "this is bad UX" outright, I tried a different approach. I mocked up three versions: his original non-dismissible banner, a dismissible banner that came back once a week, and a smaller in-context nudge that appeared inside the dashboard right next to the widget where the new feature was most relevant. I presented all three with the tradeoffs of each: visibility versus annoyance, impression count versus user satisfaction. He ended up picking the dismissible banner, which wasn't my ideal but was way better than the original ask. And he appreciated that I gave him options instead of just saying no. I think if I'd had more data, like NPS scores or user feedback about banner fatigue, I could have pushed harder. But at that point I was mostly working from design principles and intuition, which doesn't carry as much weight with a CEO.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Question: Showing options with tradeoffs is a really effective technique. You'll use that for the rest of your career. What's the hardest usability problem you've solved, and why was it hard?
Answer: The hardest one was designing a permissions system for the dashboard product. It sounds dry, but it was genuinely complex. We had three user roles: admin, manager, and viewer. Each could have different access to different sections. And the product had grown organically, so the existing permissions were inconsistent. Some sections used toggles, some used dropdowns, and one used a full matrix table that no one understood. The hard part wasn't any single screen, it was making the mental model coherent. Like, if I'm an admin setting permissions for a manager, I need to understand what that manager will see and not see. But the consequences of each permission change were invisible. You flip a toggle and... nothing visually happens. You just have to trust that somewhere, for someone else, something changed. I tried a few approaches. The one that eventually worked was a preview panel: when you adjust someone's permissions, a simplified preview of their dashboard appears on the right side showing what they'll see. It made the abstract concrete. But getting there took maybe four or five iterations. My first attempt was a big settings table which was basically the same as what we already had. My second was a role-based template system that was cleaner but didn't handle custom permission overrides. It took me a while to realize that the core problem wasn't the interface for changing permissions, it was the feedback loop. Users didn't know what their changes did. Once I reframed the problem that way, the preview panel idea clicked pretty quickly. Why it was hard: because the problem was conceptual, not visual. I could make a pretty form all day, but making an inherently abstract system feel tangible required thinking beyond layouts and into mental models. That was new territory for me.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: accessibility, design_systems, tools
Question: Permissions UX is one of those problems that looks simple until you're deep in it. The preview idea is clever. Have you ever had to design something where accessibility and visual appeal felt like they were in tension? How'd you resolve it?
Answer: Yeah. We had a card-based layout for project summaries, and the original design used a light gray text on a white background for secondary information. It looked really clean and modern, very minimal. But the contrast ratio was something like 2.5:1, which fails WCAG AA badly. You need 4.5:1 for normal text. When I darkened the text to hit the contrast requirement, the designer in me felt like it "ruined" the airy, light feel of the design. The secondary info now looked almost as prominent as the primary info, which messed with the visual hierarchy. What I ended up doing was rethinking the hierarchy instead of just changing the color. Instead of relying on color contrast alone to create hierarchy, I used size, weight, and spatial separation. I made the primary text slightly larger and bolder, kept the secondary text at accessible contrast but in a smaller size, and added more vertical spacing between the two. The hierarchy was actually stronger than the original, and it was accessible. It taught me that the "tension" between accessibility and aesthetics is usually a sign that I'm being lazy with my design tools. If the only tool I'm using for hierarchy is color lightness, I'm not using enough tools. Once I bring in typography scale, spacing, weight, and layout, I can almost always find something that's both accessible and visually sophisticated. I won't pretend I get it right every time. I still catch myself reaching for low-contrast gray text and have to stop myself. But I'm getting better at building accessible contrast into my design system defaults so I don't have to think about it per-component.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: day_in_the_life, design_handoff, prototyping, stakeholder_management, tools
Question: That reframing of hierarchy tools is spot-on. A lot of senior designers still haven't internalized that. Okay, let's talk about the day-to-day. What does a typical day or week look like for you?
Answer: A typical week for me right now is probably something like... Monday I'll review what's on the sprint board and what I need to deliver that week. I'll usually have a standup in the morning. Then I'll spend a chunk of Monday and Tuesday actually designing in Figma, heads-down work. Wednesday tends to get eaten by meetings: a design critique with the other designers, a mid-week check-in with the PM, maybe a stakeholder review. Thursday I try to protect for focused work again, that's usually when I'm refining based on feedback from Wednesday. Friday is a mix of handoff prep, documentation, and whatever I didn't finish during the week. In terms of the split, I'd say roughly 40% of my time is actual design work in Figma, maybe 15% is some form of research or analysis (looking at data, reading support tickets, reviewing session recordings), about 30% is meetings and communication (standups, critiques, stakeholder updates, Slack), and the remaining 15% is documentation and handoff work. I wish the research percentage was higher. And I wish the meetings percentage was lower. But that's the reality right now. On a good week, I can push the design time up to maybe 50% by being more protective of my calendar. On a bad week, it drops to 25% and I feel like I didn't actually produce anything.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: design_metrics, design_systems, prototyping, tools
Question: That ratio sounds pretty standard, honestly. What tools do you use daily, and how does your workflow change by project stage?
Answer: Figma is the big one, that's where I live. For early-stage work, like when I'm just exploring, I'll actually sketch on paper first or use FigJam for rough flows and spatial thinking. I find that opening Figma too early makes me think in components instead of concepts, so the low-fidelity stuff helps me stay loose. Once I'm in Figma, I'm using auto-layout and components pretty heavily. I try to build with our design system from the start so I'm not retrofitting later. For prototyping, I mostly use Figma's built-in prototyping. It's fine for click-throughs and basic flows. I've played with Framer a little for higher-fidelity interactions, but I'm not fluent enough to use it on real projects yet. For communication, it's Slack and Loom. I record a lot of Looms. When I finish a design iteration, I'll do a 3-minute Loom walking through my thinking and share it in the project channel. It's asynchronous, people can watch it when they have time, and it's way more context than a static Figma link. For research, I use Hotjar for session recordings, Mixpanel for analytics, and just Google Sheets for organizing interview notes. Nothing fancy. How the workflow changes: early in a project, I'm spending more time in FigJam and paper, writing in Notion (problem framing, assumptions, questions), and less in Figma. Mid-project, it's mostly Figma heads-down. Late in a project, it shifts to annotation, Loom walkthroughs, and sitting with engineers to answer questions.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: prototyping, stakeholder_management
Question: I like the Loom habit, that's a good async practice. How much of your role is actually designing versus communicating, aligning stakeholders, or documenting decisions?
Answer: If I'm being really honest, I'd say less than half my role is "designing" in the traditional sense of pushing pixels in Figma. And when I first started, that surprised me. I thought this job was mostly making things look good and be usable. And that is part of it, but the bigger part is everything around the design. Communicating why I made a decision takes almost as long as making the decision. Writing up my rationale in Notion, presenting options to the PM, explaining tradeoffs to engineering, getting sign-off from stakeholders. Each of those is a communication task, not a design task, but they're all essential to the design actually shipping correctly. I'd estimate maybe 35 to 40% of my time is actual design work. Another 30% is communication and alignment (meetings, Slack, Looms, presentations). Maybe 15% is documentation (specs, annotations, decision logs). And the last 15% is research and analysis. The thing I've come to appreciate is that the communication IS the design work, in a way. If I design the perfect solution but can't explain why it's right, or can't get buy-in, it doesn't matter. The design that ships is the one that everyone understands and supports, not the one that's objectively "best" in isolation.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Topics: design_systems, prototyping
Question: That's a really important realization, and one that a lot of people at your experience level haven't gotten to yet. Last question: what's the least glamorous part of your job that people outside design don't really see?
Answer: Asset management and file hygiene. It's so boring but it takes so much time. Organizing Figma files so they're navigable. Naming layers properly so engineers can inspect them. Cleaning up old iterations so the file doesn't become a graveyard of discarded ideas. Updating the design system library when someone adds a new component. Archiving pages. Making sure the file structure matches what engineering expects. Nobody posts that on Dribbble. Nobody puts "reorganized the Figma file structure for the Q3 project" in their portfolio. But if you don't do it, the file becomes unusable in about two weeks and the whole team suffers. The other unsexy thing is QA. Reviewing the implemented design against the Figma file, pixel by pixel, on multiple screen sizes, logging bugs, and then having the "is this worth fixing" negotiation with engineering for each one. Some of those bugs are genuinely important: a button that's cut off on mobile, text that overflows a container. But others are like, "this padding is 12px instead of 16px," and you have to decide whether that's worth a ticket or whether you're being precious about it. That judgment call, over and over, dozens of times per feature, is tedious and exhausting. But it's what separates a polished product from one that feels slightly off in ways users can't articulate but definitely feel.

Role: UI UX Designer
Seniority: Junior
Question: Honestly, that's one of the best answers I've gotten to that question. The QA negotiation thing is so real. Well, Jordan, this has been a great conversation. You're clearly someone who's reflective about your process, which matters more at this stage than having all the answers. We'll be in touch with next steps.
Answer: Thanks so much, Priya. I really enjoyed this. It felt more like a real conversation than an interview, which I appreciate. [End of transcript. Duration: 58 minutes.]
